Q: Which feature of C++23 allows converting std::array to std::tuple? A:

C++23 updates with the constructor and assignment operator overloads of std::tuple to accept any tuple-like argument of matching size and compatible types.

C++20, No assignment operator accepted std::array

Explain of execution statement: tup = arr;

  • Compiler checks std::array is a tuple-like object? (Yes)

  • Size matches (std::array & std::tuple have exactly 3 elements)

  • It assigns each element element-wise, equivalent to performing

std::get<i>(tup) = std::get<i>(arr) (indices 0, 1, and 2)

Q: Number of concurrent connections vs number of threads in spring boot 3 A:

Tomcat's NIO connector can accept and hold open up to 8192 TCP connections at a time (e.g., keep-alive HTTP/1.1 connections, or clients waiting on a response). But only 200 of those connections can be actively being processed by a worker thread at any given instant, because there are only 200 threads in the pool.

Q: How to combine csv files in Batch at Windows command prompt? A:

Solution for normal sized CSV

Normally for a reasonable sized CSV file the following trick should work:

>new.csv (
   type file1.csv
   more +1 file2.csv
   more +1 file3.csv
   REM etc.
)

Solution for huge CSV file

However, more is using a buffer so when there are more than 65536 lines in data, it will stop at around 65536th line and shows a prompt, which is not what we want.

So for very large CSV files we can use this alternative:

>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "Header_of_file2_csv" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "Header_of_file3_csv" file3.csv
    REM more...
)

Option /v means "not matching", option /b means matching from the beginning of line.

Proof that it works

file1.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
101,102,103
201,202,203
301,302,303

file2.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
401,402,403
501,502,503
601,602,603

file3.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
701,702,703
801,802,803
901,902,903

Command:

>new.csv (
    type file1.csv
    findstr /v /b "Col1,Col2,Col3" file2.csv
    findstr /v /b "Col1,Col2,Col3" file3.csv
)

Result from new.csv:

Col1,Col2,Col3
101,102,103
201,202,203
301,302,303
401,402,403
501,502,503
601,602,603
701,702,703
801,802,803
901,902,903

Proof that findstr will not stop at processing 65536th line of text file

If there's a concern findstr might act like more and also stops at 65536th line, we need a large file to prove (that it won't stop).

>hugefile.txt (
    REM 7000 x 10 = 70000 > 65536
    for /l %j in (1,1,7000) do @for /l %i in (0,1,9) do @echo %i
    echo last-line
)
findstr last-line hugefile.txt

findstr should print last-line immediately without delay or even any prompt.

Limitation

The command findstr /v /b pattern file will remove any matching pattern in file from output. So if there's any data row having the exact data as the header, it will also be skipped. For instance:

Col1,Col2,Col3
401,402,403
Col1,Col2,Col3
501,502,503
601,602,603

This is a very rare edge case but user of findstr needs to be aware of that.

Q: Spinning thread takes 20,000 CPU cycles to see atomic write on Xeon CPU A:

Two things inflate a figure like the 20000 cycles reported here, and both are worth ruling out before coherence traffic is blamed.

The first cause that inflates the figure is the resolution of the observing loop: PAUSE costs about 10 cycles before Skylake and as many as 140 after it, so a loop that pauses between reads can only notice a change at that granularity: latency figures.

The second cause comes from the shape of the loop itself ;-) Reading with a plain load (without a lock), and attempting the atomic operation (with a LOCK prefix or that with implicit lock such as XCHG) only once the load looks promising, keeps the waiting core from issuing locked read-modify-writes against the line the writer needs exclusively. That load-then-attempt structure is the test-test-and-set shape the Intel optimisation manual recommends, and my own FastMM4-AVX, forked from FastMM4 by Pierre le Riche, spins that way for 5000 iterations before yielding.

As it stands the number measures the obsevring loop at least as much as it measures the hardware. Three details would decide between them: (1) the loop itself, which shows how coarsely it samples and whether it isseus locked operations while waiting; (2) the thread pinning, since two hyperthreads of one core and two separate sockets differ by an order of magnitude; (3) and the C-state configuration, since waking a core out of a deep sleep state costs microseconds that owe nothing to cache coherence. A cross-socket (cross-NUMA node) transfer is a real cost, it is a different quantity from how long a loop took to notice one.

So I recommend you, as my reply, to make a real test as I suggested :-)

Q: Is it possible to load mcp servers only when a subagent is invoked? A:

You can select which MCP servers and tools a subagent can use, but AgentDefinition does not provide a documented way to delay the lifetime of an in-process server created by create_sdk_mcp_server() until that subagent runs.

AgentDefinition.mcpServers accepts server names or inline {name: config} dictionaries, while tools and disallowedTools restrict the subagetn's tool set. In the Python SDK, the field name remains camelCase. It was added in Python SDK 0.1.49, so older versions do not accept it. See the subagent reference and SDK changelog.

create_sdk_mcp_server() returns a live in-process McpSdkServerConfig, which the Python reference documents for top-level ClaudeAgentOptions.mcp_servers. The current Python SDK implementation extracts and registers in-process instances from those top-level options, separately from the serialized agent definitions. See the create_sdk_mcp_server() reference and SDK implementation.

The conservative configuration is therefore to register the in-process server at the parent level and select it by name for the subagent:

specialist_server = create_sdk_mcp_server(...)

options = ClaudeAgentOptions(
    mcp_servers={"specialist": specialist_server},
    agents={
        "specialist-agent": AgentDefinition(
            description="Use for the specialist task",
            prompt="Handle only the specialist task.",
            tools=["mcp__specialist__required_tool"],
            mcpServers=["specialist"],
        )
    },
)

This configuration limits the server and tool selection for the subagent, but it does not prove that the in-process server is constructed only when delegation occurs. Tool visibility and server lifetime are separate concerns.

If the server must be absent until the specialist runs, create a separate SDK query/client for that specialist, put only its server in that client's top-level ClaudeAgentOptions.mcp_servers, close the client when the specialist finishes. That separate client is the clear lifecycle boundary.

The context-cost premise also depends on the environment. Claude Code enables MCP tool search by default on supported models and providers, loading names and server instructions initially while deferring full schemas until use. Multiple servers can still add connection or process overhead, but they do not necessarily inject every complete schema into the initial context.

Q: Why does `stride_view<V>::iterator` have a `missing_` member even if the underlying view `V` is *not* bidirectional? A:

But the actual specification in [range.stride] makes stride_view::iterator store a missing_ member even if the iterator is not bidirectional and thus cannot move backwards.

This is false. The specification refers to missing_ as "exposition only". It is required for the exposition (how the Standard describes the functionality), but it is not required of implementations. It does not need to be stored if an implementation can achieve the same functionality through other means.
